Area.evidence_source: Similar to the experience with their parents, all participants noted that they felt disconnected from their peers. Two participants stated that in their early adolescence they started comparing themselves to their peers. This led them to define themselves as ''different'' (in terms of appearance, sexuality, academic performance, ability to regulate emotions), 'not fitting in' and 'not being understood'. For example, Mark explained: Before Grade 6 and 7 I was just running around and being a fun person, but then I actually became aware of who I am [having ginger hair, being attracted to boys] and my friends and that I couldn't change myself and all that. Then I started to think I just want to die. Seeing themselves as 'deviant' led all participants to withdraw from their peers and led two participants to seek connection with other 'deviant' peers. For example, Brian reported developing bonds with peers who 'were into the dark phase of life'. He explained: 'We were very much intrigued by death and we'd go to the graveyard and sit there. We spoke about it [suicide] a lot.' The peer group's common 'goal' was 'to die', but the group members secretly feared death. Brian was the first in the peer group to attempt suicide and the attempt gave him a sense of autonomy. He said: 'I felt proud of my actions [attempting suicide] because now I could tell my friends that I actually went through with this.'
